paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from Cangwu County in Guangxi, made in 1990 and given a long rest in [baskets](liu-bao:making-traditional). Like every [dark tea](dark:definition), its leaf was heaped after it was made, so that warmth, moisture and microbes could darken and soften it. Then it was packed tight and left to age.

Thirty-six years puts it far past the ten after which the trade counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged). Liu Bao this old is often [old stock](liu-bao:old-stock) from the years after the mining trade ended, and because its age is hard to prove, the trade reads it from the basket, the labels and the papers packed with it.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
